name: Woolly Mammoth
scare: Some mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid of Giza was being built.
description: The woolly mammoth was a cold-adapted elephant with a dense undercoat, long guard hairs and a humped fat reserve. Herds followed the dry steppe-tundra of the ice age, and their bones and frozen bodies are still found today.

name: Sabre-toothed Cat
size: ~1 m tall at the shoulder · 160–280 kg
scare: Its 28 cm sabres were built for precision killing, not bone-crushing bites.
description: Smilodon is the best-known sabre-toothed cat. Powerful forelimbs pinned prey while the jaws delivered a deep, slicing bite. Thousands of individuals were trapped in the La Brea tar pits, preserving a rare window into ice-age hunting.

name: Cave Bear
diet: Omnivore — plants, carrion and small animals
scare: Cave bears and early humans competed for the same dark caves — sometimes leaving claw marks beside paintings.
description: Cave bears were massive relatives of brown bears that denned deep in limestone caves. Their accumulated bones created the bear-cult sites that fascinated early palaeontologists, and their extinction coincides with the last ice-age cold and human pressure.

name: Woolly Rhinoceros
scare: A 39,000-year-old frozen rhino was found in Siberia with its horn and skin intact.
description: The woolly rhinoceros wore a thick double coat and a flattened front horn that may have swept snow aside while grazing. It shared the mammoth steppe with woolly mammoths, cave lions and early human hunters.

name: Irish Elk
size: ~2 m at the shoulder · 3.6 m antler span
scare: Its antlers could weigh 40 kg — the largest known of any deer.
description: Despite its name, the Irish elk was a giant deer that ranged across ice-age Eurasia. Males carried enormous palmate antlers used in display and combat. The species survived the last glacial maximum but vanished as the open steppe shrank.

name: Steppe Bison
size: ~1.8 m at the shoulder · up to 1,000 kg
scare: The mummified 'Blue Babe' bison was so fresh that a lion had been eating it when it froze 36,000 years ago.
description: The steppe bison was the ancestral form of modern bison. Herds moved across the mammoth steppe in huge numbers, and their mummified remains preserve stomach contents, parasites and even the bite marks of ice-age predators.

name: Cave Lion
diet: Carnivore — deer, horses, bison and young mammoths
scare: Cave lion cubs have been found frozen so perfectly that their fur, whiskers and claws remain.
description: The cave lion was larger than any living lion and ranged from Spain to Alaska. It appears in cave art across Europe, often as a powerful symbol. Genetic work shows it was a distinct lineage, not simply a modern lion living in caves.

name: Giant Ground Sloth
scare: Standing upright, it could reach the height of a two-storey building.
description: Megatherium was a ground-dwelling sloth the size of an elephant. It used powerful claws and a broad pelvis to rear up and pull down branches. Its extinction followed the arrival of humans and the end of the ice age in South America.

name: American Mastodon
scare: Mastodon bones have been found with human-made cut marks, showing they were hunted.
description: Mastodons were forest-dwelling proboscideans with low-crowned teeth suited to browsing. They were common in spruce and pine woodlands of ice-age North America, and their remains are often found in peat bogs and ponds.

name: Dire Wolf
scare: More than 4,000 dire wolves have been pulled from the La Brea tar pits.
description: The dire wolf was a stocky, bone-crushing canid built for taking down large prey. It was not a close relative of the modern grey wolf, and it disappeared at the end of the Pleistocene along with many of its prey species.

name: Aurochs
size: ~1.8 m at the shoulder · up to 1,000 kg
scare: The last aurochs died in a Polish forest in 1627 — a species lost within recorded history.
description: The aurochs was the wild ancestor of domestic cattle: a huge, long-horned forest and marsh grazer. Cave paintings at Lascaux show its power, and its final extinction became an early symbol of human-driven loss.

name: Glyptodon
scare: Its shell was a dome of bony plates — like a living tank the size of a car.
description: Glyptodon was a giant armadillo relative with a rigid domed carapace and a club-like tail. It lived in open habitats of ice-age South America and may have been hunted by early humans for its meat and shell.

name: Terror Bird
scare: It could likely run faster than a human and strike with a beak like a hatchet.
description: Phorusrhacids, or terror birds, were flightless predators that dominated South American ecosystems before the land bridge brought new competitors. Their powerful legs and hooked beaks made them apex hunters of open woodland.

name: Megalodon
diet: Carnivore — whales, seals and large fish
scare: A single tooth could be 18 cm long — big enough to span a human hand.
description: Megalodon was one of the largest sharks ever to live. Its serrated teeth and powerful jaws could shear through whale bone. It vanished as ocean temperatures cooled and large prey shifted, leaving only fossil teeth behind.

name: Cave Hyena
scare: Cave hyenas dragged mammoth bones into caves — and sometimes dragged human remains too.
description: The cave hyena was a cold-adapted form of spotted hyena that denned in caves across Europe and Asia. Its bone-filled lairs are important fossil sites, preserving the animals it scavenged and hunted across the mammoth steppe.

name: Grey Wolf
diet: Carnivore — deer, boar and smaller mammals
scare: A pack can coordinate a hunt across several kilometres of dark forest.
description: Wolves are the original forest ghost story: social, intelligent and almost never seen. Their howls carry for kilometres and help packs stay in touch across dense woodland after dark.

name: Barn Owl
scare: Its flight is almost silent; the only warning may be a pale shape crossing the moon.
description: Barn owls hunt by sound as much as sight, using a heart-shaped facial disc to focus faint noises. Their pale plumage and eerie screech have made them a fixture of forest folklore.

name: Common Raven
diet: Omnivore — carrion, insects, fruit and eggs
scare: Ravens remember human faces and can hold a grudge for years.
description: Ravens are among the most intelligent birds, solving puzzles and mimicking sounds. In forests they follow wolves and bears to carcasses, and their calls have carried omens in myth for thousands of years.

name: Common Vampire Bat
scare: It can walk, hop and even run along the ground to approach sleeping prey.
description: Vampire bats are the only mammals that feed entirely on blood. Their heat-sensing noses locate warm skin, and anticoagulant saliva keeps the meal flowing. They are far more specialised than they are monstrous.

name: Huntsman Spider
diet: Carnivore — insects, frogs and small lizards
size: Leg span up to 30 cm in the largest species
scare: It hunts by speed rather than webs, and some species can sprint up a tree trunk.
description: Huntsman spiders are fast, flattened hunters that live on bark and in leaf litter. Despite their size, most are harmless to humans and prefer to flee — but meeting one at night is unforgettable.

name: Firefly
diet: Larvae are predatory; adults often do not feed
scare: Some females mimic another species' flash pattern — then eat the males who answer.
description: Fireflies produce cold light through a chemical reaction in their abdomen. Their synchronised flashing turns summer forests into a living constellation, and their decline is an early warning about light pollution and habitat loss.

name: European Nightjar
scare: Its churring call has been mistaken for a distant engine or a ghost in the heath.
description: Nightjars are masters of camouflage by day and aerial hunters by night. Their enormous gape scoops moths from the dark, and their strange churring song is one of the defining sounds of a summer forest edge.

name: Black Panther
diet: Carnivore — deer, monkeys and wild pigs
scare: In the dark, the cat is invisible until its eyes catch the light.
description: Black panthers are melanistic leopards or jaguars, not a separate species. Their dark coats help them vanish in dense forest, and sightings are rare even where populations are healthy.
